line: You be shootin’ in the air like your shit looked up (Bitch)
vault_lines: You be shootin' in the air like your shit looked up (Bitch)
meaning:
Sosa is explaining here that his enemies and his opps are soft people and not fully really about the life they claim they live in reality. He does this by showing that when they shoot at him, they purposely miss, by shooting their gun off target, likely towards the sky because they don’t want to take a life, hence why he says the gun appears to have “looked up” meaning facing towards the sky.

This could be for a variety of reasons, Chief Keef’s enemies could be scared of going to jail if they get caught for murder, they may fear to live with a guilty conscience for the rest of their lives, or maybe they are just in fear of retaliation by Chief Keef and his “Glo Gang/Black Disciples” associates as the situation and beef thickens in intensity.

line: Take the magazine, now we pluggin’ like it’s hooked up
vault_lines: Take the magazine, now we pluggin' like it's hooked up
meaning:
Pluggin' has three meanings in this line. Firstly, the verb “plug”, which literally means to fill a hole or close. Sosa is saying here that he will take the magazine for his firearm and fill his enemy with holes or that he could be loading his magazine with live rounds.

Secondly, “plug” is also a slang term used to describe who can provide and supply you with all the essential things you need, most commonly used in association with drug connects. Keef is also stating he can be your plug/supplier if you do require his services.

Chief Keef strengthens his wordplay in the last sense of the term “plug”, as it is also used to name the end of an electrical appliances wire or cord, which “plugs” into a power socket usually found on the wall of a building to power our everyday devices, therefore the device would now be connected and “hooked up”.

line: You say you a killer but now we gotta push ya
vault_lines: You say you a killer but now we gotta push ya
meaning:
Chief Keef is interpolating and putting his own spin on the classic opening line from 2Pac’s “Hail Mary”.

I ain’t a killer, but don’t push me

While 2Pac uses the line to express that he is only dangerous when provoked, Keef uses the line to diss his adversary by testing their ability to live up to their own claims of being killer.

line: I’m in a fast car gettin’ T like I’m Pusha
vault_lines: I'm in a fast car gettin’ T like I'm Pusha
meaning:
Chief Keef boasts about his skills behind the wheel by claiming that he can drive while getting “T” (top), which is slang for fellatio. He finishes out the line by referencing Virginia rapper Pusha-T. Keef and Pusha previously collaborated on the remix of “Don’t Like”. Pusha also reportedly vouched for Keef to be signed to Kanye West’s G.O.O.D. Music in 2012.

line: Old school, out the window, wouldn’t make a sound
vault_lines: Old school, out the window, wouldn't make a sound
meaning:
Skengdo is referring to how in the old-school days that they used to shoot their opponents out of the window of their stolen car performing a drive-by shooting, and he’s also mentioning that they still do this act now.  The way how he described the act as “Old-school” shows that this idea was used even before he was on this road life and he got the idea from things such as old American hood movies like Paid in Full, Menace II Society, Boyz n the Hood etc.



And the fact that Skengdo describes the gun of it “wouldn’t make a sound”, meaning that he has added a silencer/supressor which is a device that reduces the sound intensity and muzzle flash when a firearm is discharged. It can be a detachable accessory to, or integral part of, the muzzle or barrel.



However, he might also be referring to him as a youth when he’d sneak out the window of his parent’s house, not making a sound to hang out with his gang or to hit the trap or even would sneak into houses robbing them and would get away with it when he was supposed to be at home, since Skengdo started road at a young age.

line: Them man there fear the kitchen (True) But that’s cool cah the corn game is different (Baow, baow)
vault_lines: Them man there fear the kitchen (True)
meaning:
“Dem man der fear the kitchen”,  refers to 410’s opponents such as 67, Harlem Spartans, KuKu etc. all fear of a Kitchen knife that 410 pulls out on them and that they all get evicted once they are confronted with the knife.



“But that’s cool, cah the corn game is different” Skengdo is saying that it’s fine to run away from the knife because most of the time he would withdraw his firearm which he mentions as “corn” which is a Bitish slang term for bullets since the projectile of a bullet looks like sweetcorn. He says that when 410 pull out their firearms at their opponents they are likely to hit them even though they are runnng since the speed of a bullet travels much faster than a human-being sprinting for their life, and this way they find it easier to get them down because with a knife they would have to chase them to harm them whereas with a gun they just have to discharge it towards them and the bullet will do their job since it penetrates through the skin even through a distance due to the high velocity.

line: Slide on ya late night like a hooker (Two 30's)
vault_lines: Slide on ya late night like a hooker (Two 30’s)

The stereotype surrounding hookers and prostitutes is that they can often be found late night in cities around street corners and in red light districts waiting to attract a punters attention so they can have sex to earn cash, often placed or posted there by a pimp or working on their own accord.

Chief Keef is saying he will stay posted in his opps area late at night (much like a hooker would) waiting to see an enemy, so when he does he can ‘slide’ on them, which means to pull up on them and attack them in a drive-by shooting.

line: Let it go tlil ain’t no more like my shit booked up (Diamonds)
vault_lines: Let it go tlil ain't no more like my shit booked up (Diamonds)
meaning:
Chief Keef compares the release of bullets from his firearm of choice to his tour, gig, and performance bookings.

When a tour is sold out due to high demand from fans wanting to see the performer live in action, then the performer will be very busy for those few months and won’t have much time for anything else, and there won’t be any tour dates left to book a ticket for, hence Chief Keef would be “booked up”.

He’s explaining here that he will rapidly fire his gun at his enemies until there are no rounds or bullets left inside the weapon, as quick as a high profile in demand artist sells out a tour, showing the severity of how much he wants to catch that person with one of said bullets.

line: Boop-boop-boop-boop, that’s a tre pound And now you’re thinkin’ that you shoulda never came out
meaning:
“Tre Pound” is slang for a revolver or pistol, in particular, a .357 calibre firearm which is shortened to .35 . “Tre” deriving from the number “three” in Italian and Spanish, and “pound” representing “5”.

AM is stating that when people around him who aren’t built for the type of lifestyle he lives hear the sound of his “Tre Pound” discharging, they’ll be  filled with fear and disbelief that they’ll wish they never got involved with him; or in his enemies case, wish they never beefed him in the first place.
